At ground level, there are five portals under arched openings.[98][172] The largest of those is the center portal, called the Portal of Paradise, which contains carvings of the transfiguration of Jesus as well as St. John and 32 biblical characters;[219] these were carved in 1988 under Simon Verity's leadership.[175] St. John is depicted on the trumeau, or vertical pier, between the two pairs of doors within the center portal.[220] The center portal also contains depictions of New York City skyscrapers being destroyed in an apocalypse.[221] The center, northernmost, and southernmost portals are set within large, gabled structures with several archivolts, or arched moldings, surrounding each portal under the gables; porches overhang the portals above the gables. The other two portals are located under simple rectangular canopy structures,[172][175] located underneath grisaille windows looking into the nave.[218] Lights salvaged from the former Pennsylvania Station illuminate the steps in front of the portals.[175]

Title: 32 reactions · 3 comments | The most beautiful room in the New York City subway has been locked since December 31, 1945 — and most New Yorkers have ridden past it without ever knowing it was there. 🏛️

When the IRT opened in 1904, City Hall station was its architectural masterpiece. Heins and LaFarge — the same architects behind the Cathedral of Saint John the Divine — designed its soaring tiled arches, brass chandeliers, and natural skylights with the same reverence they might give a sacred space. It was a statement: this city's underground would be magnificent. 🌟

But by 1945, the curved platform couldn't accommodate the longer train cars a growing city needed, and the MTA sealed it and walked away. Today it still sits beneath City Hall Park, preserved almost exactly as it was on the day it closed — peeling paint over intact tilework, skylights still filtering a sliver of light into the dark. The Transit Museum has offered rare tours over the years, and those who have been inside describe it as one of the most haunting and beautiful spaces in the entire city. 🗝️

[He arrived in New York in 1784 with a suitcase of musical instruments and almost no money. Within sixty years, John Jacob Astor had become the richest man in America — not by building anything, not by inventing anything, but by quietly buying the island of Manhattan, one lot at a time. 🏙️ Astor's genius was recognizing something no one else had clearly articulated: land in Manhattan was finite, and New York was already running out of it. While other merchants chased fur and shipping and trade, Astor turned his profits into ground leases — long, patient contracts that let buildings go up on his land while he sat back and collected rent, decade after decade, generation after generation. He bought land uptown when everyone thought uptown was too far from the action. He held it. He waited. The city grew toward him. By the time he died in 1848, his estate was worth around twenty million dollars — the largest private fortune in American history at that point, built almost entirely from the ground beneath other people's feet. 💰 The Astor family name eventually faded from New York the way all great fortunes do, through death duties and divorce and bad timing and the passage of time. But the system Astor invented — the ground lease, the patient accumulation of unremarkable-looking Manhattan blocks — is still running beneath the city today. A remarkable proportion of Manhattan's midtown and upper west side real estate traces back, through decades of transfer, to bets he placed before the Civil War.

That school was torn down and is an empty lot (still). Fredolin Hartman, a Bavarian immigrant, settled in Ventura and purchased a lot on Main and Palm up to Poli. He started Ventura Brewery at the top of Palm, and in 1888, built the ‘Anacapa Hotel’ on the corner, where Top Hat is. The Rose Hotel opened in 1890 on Main and Chestnut, where Dargans is. Built by a wealthy Pasadena businessman who had big development plans, but ended up bankrupt. Renamed the Hotel De Leon, was torn down in 1934. The Mitchell Block - the Mitchell brothers immigrated to Ventura from Ireland and made a living making bricks. They bought up the block on Meta St between Chestnut and Fir and built two houses that are still standing today! The city limits ended at San Jon - This is where the Thompson Ranch started. In 1860, Dixie M. Thompson bought 1/2 of Rancho San Miguel, 2,400 acres along the coast and over the bluffs. He became a lima bean producer - one of the world’s largest ranches, which was later subdivided into the Buenaventura Tract. # The most beautiful room in the New York City subway has been locked since December 31, 1945 — and most New Yorkers have ridden past it without ever knowing it was there. 🏛️ When the IRT opened in 1904, City Hall station was its architectural masterpiece. Heins and LaFarge — the same architects behind the Cathedral of Saint John the Divine — designed its soaring tiled arches, brass chandeliers, and natural skylights with the same reverence they might give a sacred space. It was a statement: this city's underground would be magnificent. 🌟 But by 1945, the curved platform couldn't accommodate the longer train cars a growing city needed, and the MTA sealed it and walked away. Today it still sits beneath City Hall Park, preserved almost exactly as it was on the day it closed — peeling paint over intact tilework, skylights still filtering a sliver of light into the dark. The Transit Museum has offered rare tours over the years, and those who have been inside describe it as one of the most haunting and beautiful spaces in the entire city. 🗝️ #EmpireState #NewYorkCity #SubwaySecrets #NYCHistory #LostNewYork | Empire State Chronicles | Facebook

opened.anchor: A Cathedral Built With Melted-Down Nazi Tanks
opened.information:
Source: https://arkeonews.net/a-cathedral-built-with-melted-down-nazi-tanks/
Title: A Cathedral Built With Melted-Down Nazi Tanks
Chunks: 0,1,2
Express · 20 September 2026   
By Leman Altuntaş 3 min read
Beneath the feet of visitors entering a monumental cathedral near Moscow lies an unusual piece of World War IIhistory: metal recovered from NaziGermany’s defeated military. The Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces incorporates melted-down German tank tracks into its entrance steps, turning captured weapons into a permanent part of a religious building.
Explore Churches
The extraordinary detail is not a legend. It was confirmed by Russia’s then-defence minister, Sergei Shoigu, during the cathedral’s construction.

## Walking on the Weapons of a Defeated Army
Located in Patriot Park in Kubinka, outside Moscow, the cathedral was built to commemorate the 75th anniversary of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany.
In March 2020, Shoigu explained that tracks from German tanks had been incorporated into an alloy used to manufacture the cathedral’s steps. The symbolism was deliberate: visitors would enter the building by walking over the weapons of an army defeated in 1945.
New · Official Arkeonews App
The latest archaeology news, discoveries, ancient civilizations and cultural heritage stories, wherever you go.
Visit Dig Sites
Get it on Google Play
The project involved more than tank components. Russian officials had announced plans to use captured Wehrmacht weapons, including military equipment preserved in Defence Ministry stockpiles. The resulting metal was incorporated into the entrance steps, while captured German armaments were also used in metal flooring inside the cathedral.
The idea of incorporating captured enemy weapons into religious architecture was not entirely new. In St. Petersburg, the Transfiguration Cathedralis surrounded by a fence made from 102 Ottoman cannon barrels captured during the Russo-Turkish War of 1828–1829. At Kubinka, the same symbolism took a different form: the weapons were melted down and became part of the building itself.
Explore Churches
The use of wartime remnants in religious architecture has a parallel in Britain. After German bombs destroyed Coventry Cathedralin 1940, three nails recovered from its ruined roof were fashioned into a cross, becoming a symbol of reconciliation. At Kubinka, however, the message was different: weapons taken from a defeated enemy became part of a monument to military victory.
The Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces in daylight. Credit: Alexander Motin / Wikimedia Commons.

## A Cathedral Designed Around the Year 1945
Its dark green exterior, monumental domes and elaborate mosaics reflect the cathedral’s dual identity as an Orthodox place of worship and a memorial to Russian military history. Even its dimensions contain references to the war.
Explore Churches
The central dome’s drum measures 19.45 metres in diameter, representing the year 1945. The bell tower stands 75 metres high, marking the victory’s 75th anniversary, while a smaller dome reaches 14.18 metres, commemorating the 1,418 days of the Soviet-German
Dedicated to the Resurrection of Christ, the cathedral was consecrated by Patriarch Kirill on June 14, 2020. It forms part of a wider memorial complex that includes exhibitions documenting the Soviet war effort.
The German tank tracks embedded in its steps give that commemoration a physical dimension. More than eight decades after the war, material once used to propel Nazi armoured vehicles remains beneath the feet of people entering Russia’s principal military cathedral.
Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ (Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces). Credit: Wikimedia Commons
Russian news agency Interfax
Russian Orthodox Church – Consecration of the Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces (June 14, 2020)

# Consecrated 1945 Cathedral
[[](https://www.instagram.com/cassiainrussia) cassiainrussia 2,432 The Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces,also known as the Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ,is a Russian Orthodox Patriarchal cathedral in honour of the Resurrection of Christ and « dedicated to the 75th anniversary of victory in the Great Patriotic War, as well as the military feats of the Russian people in all wars », built in the Patriot Park in the Odintsovsky District, Moscow Oblast. According to the official website, « the church was designed in a monumental Russian style, organically incorporating modern architectural approaches and innovations unique to the Orthodox church creation ». The façades of the building are finished with metal, the arches are glazed. The walls of the church, decorated with murals, include battle scenes from Russian military history and Bible scripture texts. The decoration of the lower (small) church is made of ceramics and is decorated with Gzhel painting, with pieces of glass smalt used in the manufacture of the mosaic panels. The central apse dedicated to the Resurrection of Christ is metal relief. 🙏❤️](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DV5jdGJCPOH/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)
